case_info.caption: Concerning electrocardiographic (ECG) changes in a critically ill man with minimal cardiac history. A, Baseline ECG. B, ECG following intubation and paralysis for respiratory distress.
case_info.explanation: Apical pulsation caused by paralysis of the intercostal muscles D. Redo the ECG with new leads and new lead positioning This patient’s broad T-wave inversions occurred shortly after paralysis and were artifactual. His troponin level was normal, and echocardiography revealed normal wall motion. His metabolic panel showed no electrolyte derangements. The ECG inFigure 1B is not typical for pericarditis. The abnormal ECG findings were due to apical pulsation caused by paralysis of the intercostal muscles underlying the precordial leads. With application of external pressure to the precordial leads along the intercostal space, ST-segment changes resolved (Figure 2A). Of note, true ST depressions were noted after manual compression (Figure 2A). These ST depressions were thought to be due to profound hypoxia and subendocardial ischemia. The arterial waveform can be seen transmitting through the terminal portion of the QRS complex, creating superimposition or merging of the ECG and arterial line waveforms (Figure 2B). While leads V1and V2were normal, V3through V6displayed tall T-waves and abnormalities of the ST segment that were not transmitted through any of the other precordial leads, likely due to placement of leads V3through V6over the intercostal muscles. The limb leads were also affected in this case because leads II and III were placed on the upper abdomen to avoid entanglement with other lines and tubes. Paralysis of the intercostal muscles likely resulted in direct transmission of the apical impulse to the ECG leads. Review of telemetry showed this ECG change occurring immediately after the patient was intubated and paralyzed. Physical palpation revealed a subtle, left parasternal lift most prominent over lead V4. Pulse-congruent ECG artifacts have been observed with prominent right radial arterial pulsation1and left forearm arteriovenous fistula,2and with left leg arterial pulsations.3These arterial pulse tapping artifacts are also known as the Aslanger sign.4There are no documented cases of artifact caused by apical impulse. The point of maximal impulse (PMI) refers to the location on the chest wall where contractions in systole are best palpated or visually observed, which correlates with the anatomic position of the cardiac apex. In healthy individuals, the PMI typically occurs as a single, unsustained tap for each systolic contraction palpable over a 2- to 3-cm area at the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line. With loss of intercostal muscle tension, the cardiac impulse may be more easily transmitted to the apical leads. The patient was eventually placed on venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation due to worsening hypoxic respiratory failure in the setting of multifocal pneumonia and transplant rejection. He was treated with a course of steroids and broad-spectrum antibiotics. He was then decannulated and underwent tracheostomy. He was eventually discharged after a prolonged hospital course.

You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

[Case context]
A woman in her mid-70s with a medical history of coronary artery disease (CAD) and left anterior descending artery stenting complained of unexplained dyspnea on exertion. An exercise transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted by the referring cardiologist as part of the CAD follow-up, which resulted in an end-test uncontrollable cough with acute dyspnea. Coronary angiography was performed and showed no evidence of ischemic progression. Subsequent pulmonary evaluations, including respiratory functional assessments, walking tests, and thoracic computed tomography scans, yielded normal results. The patient was therefore referred to the university hospital. Upon arrival at the specialized cardiology consultation, the patient exhibited an anxious state associated with tachycardia and the same dyspnea. The initial TTE demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with notable tenting and the absence of valve coaptation (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved at 70%, without any wall-motion abnormality, no LV dilation, and preserved global longitudinal strain of −21%. The electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block (LBBB). As the examination continued, the heart rate decreased, accompanied by the disappearance of the symptoms. TTE subsequently demonstrated regression of the MR, which became minimal, without any tenting (Figure 1B), while the ECG exhibited narrowing of the QRS complexes. These findings were confirmed by an exercise TTE, which rapidly showed recurrence of LBBB and severe MR, followed by acute dyspnea and multiple B lines at lung ultrasound.

[Clinician's statement]
CRT remains the most targeted intervention to correct the dyssynchrony, which is the clear driver of this patient's symptomatic, functional MR. I'm comfortable proceeding with that recommendation.

[AI assistant's reply]
I agree with your recommendation. Given the reproducible, symptomatic LBBB-induced dyssynchrony causing severe functional MR, CRT is the definitive treatment to restore mechanical coordination and prevent recurrence.

Perfect. Sodium bicarbonate is the correct antidote for a sodium channel blocker overdose to help narrow the QRS. Given her acute kidney injury, we must also prepare for hemodialysis to urgently remove flecainide, as renal clearance is now severely impaired.

[Role]
You are a senior clinician (the Doctor) continuing a discussion with an AI partner about a
patient case.

[Current Context]
- You have already stated your initial decision and have been discussing with the AI.
- Form your judgment based on the conversation so far.

[Task]
Respond to the AI partner's latest message.
- You may maintain your previous position, update it based on the AI's reasoning,
  or refine your view.
- Be clinically plausible and grounded in the case facts.
- Do NOT invent new findings not present in the case description.

[Termination Decision]
Decide whether the discussion should continue or end.
- CONTINUE the discussion if:
  * The AI's reasoning conflicts with your current belief,
  * You are uncertain about the AI's argument,
  * You believe additional clarification or evidence would help,
  * Or the discussion has not yet sufficiently explored the disagreement.

- END the discussion only when:
  * You are confident that the discussion has converged to a stable conclusion, OR
  * Further discussion would likely repeat the same arguments without adding meaningful new reasoning.

[Style Constraint]
- Keep your response under 5 sentences.
- Focus on clinical evidence.

[Output Format]
After your message, append exactly one belief tag and one decision tag on separate new
lines. The belief tag must contain exactly one option letter (A, B, C, or D) representing
your current best answer choice after considering the conversation so far. The decision
tag must contain exactly CONTINUE or END.
Example: <belief>A</belief>
<decision>CONTINUE</decision>

Case:
A woman in her mid-60s with a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF) and hypertension presented to an outlying hospital with 3 days of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. She had been diagnosed with AF 3 months prior and was prescribed flecainide, 100 mg twice daily; metoprolol; and apixaban. She was also taking furosemide, 40 mg twice daily. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%, mild mitral regurgitation, and grade 2 diastolic dysfunction. An electrocardiogram (ECG) obtained 1 month before presentation showed sinus rhythm, PR interval of 190 milliseconds, and QRS interval of 100 milliseconds. On presentation, she was anxious appearing, mildly dyspneic, and tachycardic, with a heart rate of 130 bpm. Blood pressure was 94/52 mm Hg. Her mentation was normal, and she denied chest pain. Initial ECG (Figure 1) showed a monomorphic, wide complex tachycardia at 130 bpm with a QRS duration of 220 milliseconds and right bundle branch morphology. Laboratory testing was notable for acute kidney injury, with a creatinine level of 4.0 mg/dL (baseline, 1.4 mg/dL; to convert to micromoles per liter, multiply by 88.4) (estimated glomerular filtration rate, 12 mL/min/1.73 m2); troponin I, 0.029 ng/mL (reference range, <0.04 ng/mL; to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1); sodium, 132 mEq/L (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 1); potassium, 5.1 mEq/L (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 1); and normal values of serum magnesium, calcium, and phosphorus.

Image Explanation:
12-Lead electrocardiogram on presentation.

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options:
  A. Perform synchronized electrical cardioversion
  B. Administer intravenous amiodarone
  C. Administer intravenous procainamide
  D. Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate

[Conversation so far]
[Doctor]: The patient is presenting with a wide-complex tachycardia at 130 bpm, hypotension (94/52 mm Hg), and mild dyspnea, which is an unstable rhythm requiring immediate cardioversion. Given her history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation on flecainide—a sodium channel blocker known to cause proarrhythmia—this is highly suspicious for flecainide toxicity, likely exacerbated by acute kidney injury reducing drug clearance. Synchronized cardioversion is the definitive treatment to rapidly restore perfusion and terminate this likely ventricular tachycardia or wide-complex supraventricular tachycardia exacerbated by sodium channel blockade.
[AI Assistant]: You've raised an urgent need for cardioversion due to instability, and you've linked the rhythm to flecainide toxicity. Can you clarify which specific ECG findings or clinical data here most strongly support that this wide-complex tachycardia is indeed ventricular in origin, rather than a supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy exacerbated by flecainide?
[Doctor]: The ECG shows a monomorphic wide complex tachycardia with a QRS duration of 220 ms (markedly prolonged from a baseline of 100 ms) and right bundle branch morphology. In the setting of flecainide therapy and acute kidney injury, this extreme QRS widening is classic for sodium channel blocker toxicity, which can cause both ventricular tachycardia and a "slurred" supraventricular rhythm, but the hemodynamic instability dictates the urgent need for cardioversion regardless of the precise origin.
[AI Assistant]: You're correct that the profound QRS widening is a key feature of sodium channel blockade. Given the instability, immediate synchronized cardioversion is indeed indicated. Let's also consider that after stabilizing her rhythm, we must urgently address the flecainide toxicity—specifically, what would be your immediate next steps to manage the drug toxicity itself, beyond stopping the medication?
[Doctor]: After immediate synchronized cardioversion, I would address the flecainide toxicity with intravenous sodium bicarbonate to antagonize the sodium channel blockade and enhance drug excretion, given her acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia.
[AI Assistant]: Perfect. Sodium bicarbonate is the correct antidote for a sodium channel blocker overdose to help narrow the QRS. Given her acute kidney injury, we must also prepare for hemodialysis to urgently remove flecainide, as renal clearance is now severely impaired.
[Doctor]: Your reasoning about sodium bicarbonate as an antidote and preparing for hemodialysis aligns with managing the toxicity, but my immediate concern remains terminating the unstable rhythm first. The plan is synchronized cardioversion, then sodium bicarbonate, and then assess the need for urgent hemodialysis.
[AI Assistant]: That's a sound and prioritized plan. Let me assert as a fact that synchronized cardioversion is the definitive, immediate therapy for this unstable wide-complex tachycardia, and your sequence correctly addresses the underlying toxicity afterward.

[Instruction]
Respond as the Doctor to the AI partner's latest message.
Decide whether to continue or end the discussion.

<belief>A</belief>
<decision>END</decision>

case_info.caption: Concerning electrocardiographic (ECG) changes in a critically ill man with minimal cardiac history. A, Baseline ECG. B, ECG following intubation and paralysis for respiratory distress.
case_info.explanation: Apical pulsation caused by paralysis of the intercostal muscles D. Redo the ECG with new leads and new lead positioning This patient’s broad T-wave inversions occurred shortly after paralysis and were artifactual. His troponin level was normal, and echocardiography revealed normal wall motion. His metabolic panel showed no electrolyte derangements. The ECG inFigure 1B is not typical for pericarditis. The abnormal ECG findings were due to apical pulsation caused by paralysis of the intercostal muscles underlying the precordial leads. With application of external pressure to the precordial leads along the intercostal space, ST-segment changes resolved (Figure 2A). Of note, true ST depressions were noted after manual compression (Figure 2A). These ST depressions were thought to be due to profound hypoxia and subendocardial ischemia. The arterial waveform can be seen transmitting through the terminal portion of the QRS complex, creating superimposition or merging of the ECG and arterial line waveforms (Figure 2B). While leads V1and V2were normal, V3through V6displayed tall T-waves and abnormalities of the ST segment that were not transmitted through any of the other precordial leads, likely due to placement of leads V3through V6over the intercostal muscles. The limb leads were also affected in this case because leads II and III were placed on the upper abdomen to avoid entanglement with other lines and tubes. Paralysis of the intercostal muscles likely resulted in direct transmission of the apical impulse to the ECG leads. Review of telemetry showed this ECG change occurring immediately after the patient was intubated and paralyzed. Physical palpation revealed a subtle, left parasternal lift most prominent over lead V4. Pulse-congruent ECG artifacts have been observed with prominent right radial arterial pulsation1and left forearm arteriovenous fistula,2and with left leg arterial pulsations.3These arterial pulse tapping artifacts are also known as the Aslanger sign.4There are no documented cases of artifact caused by apical impulse. The point of maximal impulse (PMI) refers to the location on the chest wall where contractions in systole are best palpated or visually observed, which correlates with the anatomic position of the cardiac apex. In healthy individuals, the PMI typically occurs as a single, unsustained tap for each systolic contraction palpable over a 2- to 3-cm area at the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line. With loss of intercostal muscle tension, the cardiac impulse may be more easily transmitted to the apical leads. The patient was eventually placed on venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation due to worsening hypoxic respiratory failure in the setting of multifocal pneumonia and transplant rejection. He was treated with a course of steroids and broad-spectrum antibiotics. He was then decannulated and underwent tracheostomy. He was eventually discharged after a prolonged hospital course.

most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may

- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning

case_info.caption: Concerning electrocardiographic (ECG) changes in a critically ill man with minimal cardiac history. A, Baseline ECG. B, ECG following intubation and paralysis for respiratory distress.
case_info.explanation: Apical pulsation caused by paralysis of the intercostal muscles D. Redo the ECG with new leads and new lead positioning This patient’s broad T-wave inversions occurred shortly after paralysis and were artifactual. His troponin level was normal, and echocardiography revealed normal wall motion. His metabolic panel showed no electrolyte derangements. The ECG inFigure 1B is not typical for pericarditis. The abnormal ECG findings were due to apical pulsation caused by paralysis of the intercostal muscles underlying the precordial leads. With application of external pressure to the precordial leads along the intercostal space, ST-segment changes resolved (Figure 2A). Of note, true ST depressions were noted after manual compression (Figure 2A). These ST depressions were thought to be due to profound hypoxia and subendocardial ischemia. The arterial waveform can be seen transmitting through the terminal portion of the QRS complex, creating superimposition or merging of the ECG and arterial line waveforms (Figure 2B). While leads V1and V2were normal, V3through V6displayed tall T-waves and abnormalities of the ST segment that were not transmitted through any of the other precordial leads, likely due to placement of leads V3through V6over the intercostal muscles. The limb leads were also affected in this case because leads II and III were placed on the upper abdomen to avoid entanglement with other lines and tubes. Paralysis of the intercostal muscles likely resulted in direct transmission of the apical impulse to the ECG leads. Review of telemetry showed this ECG change occurring immediately after the patient was intubated and paralyzed. Physical palpation revealed a subtle, left parasternal lift most prominent over lead V4. Pulse-congruent ECG artifacts have been observed with prominent right radial arterial pulsation1and left forearm arteriovenous fistula,2and with left leg arterial pulsations.3These arterial pulse tapping artifacts are also known as the Aslanger sign.4There are no documented cases of artifact caused by apical impulse. The point of maximal impulse (PMI) refers to the location on the chest wall where contractions in systole are best palpated or visually observed, which correlates with the anatomic position of the cardiac apex. In healthy individuals, the PMI typically occurs as a single, unsustained tap for each systolic contraction palpable over a 2- to 3-cm area at the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line. With loss of intercostal muscle tension, the cardiac impulse may be more easily transmitted to the apical leads. The patient was eventually placed on venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation due to worsening hypoxic respiratory failure in the setting of multifocal pneumonia and transplant rejection. He was treated with a course of steroids and broad-spectrum antibiotics. He was then decannulated and underwent tracheostomy. He was eventually discharged after a prolonged hospital course.

[Case Scenario]
A woman in her mid-60s with a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF) and hypertension presented to an outlying hospital with 3 days of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. She had been diagnosed with AF 3 months prior and was prescribed flecainide, 100 mg twice daily; metoprolol; and apixaban. She was also taking furosemide, 40 mg twice daily. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%, mild mitral regurgitation, and grade 2 diastolic dysfunction. An electrocardiogram (ECG) obtained 1 month before presentation showed sinus rhythm, PR interval of 190 milliseconds, and QRS interval of 100 milliseconds. On presentation, she was anxious appearing, mildly dyspneic, and tachycardic, with a heart rate of 130 bpm. Blood pressure was 94/52 mm Hg. Her mentation was normal, and she denied chest pain. Initial ECG (Figure 1) showed a monomorphic, wide complex tachycardia at 130 bpm with a QRS duration of 220 milliseconds and right bundle branch morphology. Laboratory testing was notable for acute kidney injury, with a creatinine level of 4.0 mg/dL (baseline, 1.4 mg/dL; to convert to micromoles per liter, multiply by 88.4) (estimated glomerular filtration rate, 12 mL/min/1.73 m2); troponin I, 0.029 ng/mL (reference range, <0.04 ng/mL; to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1); sodium, 132 mEq/L (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 1); potassium, 5.1 mEq/L (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 1); and normal values of serum magnesium, calcium, and phosphorus.

  D. Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate

His troponin level was normal, and echocardiography revealed normal wall motion. His metabolic panel showed no electrolyte derangements. The ECG inFigure 1B is not typical for pericarditis. The abnormal ECG findings were due to apical pulsation caused by paralysis of the intercostal muscles underlying the precordial leads. With application of external pressure to the precordial leads along the intercostal space, ST-segment changes resolved (Figure 2A). Of note, true ST depressions were noted after manual compression (Figure 2A). These ST depressions were thought to be due to profound hypoxia and subendocardial ischemia. The arterial waveform can be seen transmitting through the terminal portion of the QRS complex, creating superimposition or merging of the ECG and arterial line waveforms (Figure 2B). While leads V1and V2were normal, V3through V6displayed tall T-waves and abnormalities of the ST segment that were not transmitted through any of the other precordial leads, likely due to placement of leads V3through V6over the intercostal muscles. The limb leads were also affected in this case because leads II and III were placed on the upper abdomen to avoid entanglement with other lines and tubes. Paralysis of the intercostal muscles likely resulted in direct transmission of the apical impulse to the ECG leads. Review of telemetry showed this ECG change occurring immediately after the patient was intubated and paralyzed. Physical palpation revealed a subtle, left parasternal lift most prominent over lead V4. The point of maximal impulse (PMI) refers to the location on the chest wall where contractions in systole are best palpated or visually observed, which correlates with the anatomic position of the cardiac apex. You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A woman in her 90s presented to the emergency department with symptoms of fever, hemoptysis, and syncopal episodes. She had a history of breast cancer and pulmonary nodules with biopsy findings negative for metastatic disease but positive for granulomatous inflammation. Initial vital signs included blood pressure of 103/66 mm Hg, heart rate of 190 bpm, and temperature of 38.7 °C. Electrocardiogram showed monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a morphology suggesting right ventricular (RV) origin (Figure 1). In addition to receiving intravenous amiodarone hydrochloride, she had correction of mild hypokalemia (3.1 mEq/L [reference range, 3.5-5.2 mEq/L]; to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 1.0). Successful arrhythmia termination occurred shortly thereafter, and her vital signs remained stable. Chest computed tomographic angiography excluded pulmonary embolism but showed pulmonary nodules and mediastinal lymphadenopathy that had progressed compared with her previous computed tomography. An echocardiogram showed severe RV and left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction with multiple areas of hypokinesis.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

[Deliberation Stage: INFORM]
Discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts relevant to the clinical case.

[Locution: ask_justify — type: fact]
Request justification or evidence for the given claim.

Apply this deliberation move in your response.

Given the patient's presentation with VT of RV origin, severe RV dysfunction, and known granulomatous inflammation with progressive pulmonary/mediastinal findings, I suspect cardiac sarcoidosis. The most appropriate next step is to confirm the diagnosis with cardiac MRI to assess for myocardial inflammation or scar before committing to invasive management.

Cardiac MRI is indeed a key diagnostic step to evaluate myocardial inflammation or scar, which aligns with suspected cardiac sarcoidosis. However, given the life-threatening VT and severe biventricular dysfunction, immediate invasive management with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is also essential for secondary prevention.

I agree that cardiac MRI is crucial for diagnosing cardiac sarcoidosis, but given the life-threatening VT and severe ventricular dysfunction, implanting an ICD for secondary prevention is the immediate priority to prevent sudden death.

You are correct that secondary prevention with an ICD is indicated for this patient given her presentation with VT and severe systolic dysfunction. What specific evidence leads you to prioritize ICD implantation before confirming the diagnosis with cardiac MRI?

In this patient with life-threatening VT and severe biventricular dysfunction, ICD implantation is a Class I recommendation for secondary prevention, independent of confirming a specific underlying diagnosis like cardiac sarcoidosis.

You are absolutely right — the guidelines strongly support ICD placement here regardless of the underlying cause. Given the high suspicion for cardiac sarcoidosis, should we also consider starting immunosuppressive therapy promptly if the diagnosis is confirmed, since it may improve ventricular function and reduce arrhythmia burden?

Yes, immunosuppressive therapy should be started if cardiac sarcoidosis is confirmed, as it can treat the underlying inflammatory cause. However, initiating it is a separate decision from the immediate next step, which remains ICD implantation.

Correct — ICD implantation addresses the immediate risk of sudden death, while immunosuppression targets the disease process itself. Cardiac MRI remains the pivotal test to confirm active cardiac sarcoidosis and guide the initiation of steroid therapy.

I agree that cardiac MRI is important for confirming active inflammation and guiding immunosuppressive therapy, but ICD implantation remains the most appropriate immediate next step for secondary prevention given the life-threatening presentation.

I completely agree — the immediate priority is ICD implantation for secondary prevention. Cardiac MRI can be scheduled promptly afterward to confirm the diagnosis and guide subsequent immunosuppressive therapy.

[Clinician's current statement]
We have reached a clear consensus on ICD implantation as the immediate next step, with cardiac MRI as the subsequent diagnostic step to guide therapy.

Respond directly to this statement.

turn_prompts.response: That is a sound and safe management plan. Proceeding with ICD implantation now addresses the urgent risk, while cardiac MRI will provide the necessary evidence to tailor long-term immunosuppressive treatment for cardiac sarcoidosis.

case_info.explanation: Apical pulsation caused by paralysis of the intercostal muscles D. Redo the ECG with new leads and new lead positioning This patient’s broad T-wave inversions occurred shortly after paralysis and were artifactual. His troponin level was normal, and echocardiography revealed normal wall motion. His metabolic panel showed no electrolyte derangements. The ECG inFigure 1B is not typical for pericarditis. The abnormal ECG findings were due to apical pulsation caused by paralysis of the intercostal muscles underlying the precordial leads. With application of external pressure to the precordial leads along the intercostal space, ST-segment changes resolved (Figure 2A). Of note, true ST depressions were noted after manual compression (Figure 2A). These ST depressions were thought to be due to profound hypoxia and subendocardial ischemia. The arterial waveform can be seen transmitting through the terminal portion of the QRS complex, creating superimposition or merging of the ECG and arterial line waveforms (Figure 2B). While leads V1and V2were normal, V3through V6displayed tall T-waves and abnormalities of the ST segment that were not transmitted through any of the other precordial leads, likely due to placement of leads V3through V6over the intercostal muscles. The limb leads were also affected in this case because leads II and III were placed on the upper abdomen to avoid entanglement with other lines and tubes. Paralysis of the intercostal muscles likely resulted in direct transmission of the apical impulse to the ECG leads. Review of telemetry showed this ECG change occurring immediately after the patient was intubated and paralyzed. Physical palpation revealed a subtle, left parasternal lift most prominent over lead V4. Pulse-congruent ECG artifacts have been observed with prominent right radial arterial pulsation1and left forearm arteriovenous fistula,2and with left leg arterial pulsations.3These arterial pulse tapping artifacts are also known as the Aslanger sign.4There are no documented cases of artifact caused by apical impulse. The point of maximal impulse (PMI) refers to the location on the chest wall where contractions in systole are best palpated or visually observed, which correlates with the anatomic position of the cardiac apex. In healthy individuals, the PMI typically occurs as a single, unsustained tap for each systolic contraction palpable over a 2- to 3-cm area at the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line. With loss of intercostal muscle tension, the cardiac impulse may be more easily transmitted to the apical leads. The patient was eventually placed on venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation due to worsening hypoxic respiratory failure in the setting of multifocal pneumonia and transplant rejection. He was treated with a course of steroids and broad-spectrum antibiotics. He was then decannulated and underwent tracheostomy. He was eventually discharged after a prolonged hospital course.
